questions.question_html: The relative lowering of vapour pressure produced by dissolving $18$ g of urea (Molar mass $=60\text{g mol}^{-1}$ ) in $100$ g of water is
questions.explanation_text: For a non-volatile solute like urea, the relative lowering of vapour pressure is equal to the mole fraction of the solute. $\frac{p^{\circ}-p}{p^{\circ}}=x_{\text{solute}}$ Moles of urea: $n_{\text{urea}}=\frac{18}{60}=0.3\text{mol}$ Moles of water: $n_{\text{water}}=\frac{100}{18}=5.56\text{mol}$ Now, mole fraction of urea is $x_{\text{urea}}=\frac{n_{\text{urea}}}{n_{\text{urea}}+n_{\text{water}}}$ $x_{\text{urea}}=\frac{0.3}{0.3+5.56}$ $x_{\text{urea}}=\frac{0.3}{5.86}=0.051$ So, the relative lowering of vapour pressure is $0.051$ Correct option: Option C.
questions.explanation_html:
For a non-volatile solute like urea, the relative lowering of vapour pressure is equal to the mole fraction of the solute.

$\frac{p^{\circ}-p}{p^{\circ}}=x_{\text{solute}}$

Moles of urea:

$n_{\text{urea}}=\frac{18}{60}=0.3\text{mol}$

Moles of water:

$n_{\text{water}}=\frac{100}{18}=5.56\text{mol}$

Now, mole fraction of urea is

$x_{\text{urea}}=\frac{n_{\text{urea}}}{n_{\text{urea}}+n_{\text{water}}}$

$x_{\text{urea}}=\frac{0.3}{0.3+5.56}$

$x_{\text{urea}}=\frac{0.3}{5.86}=0.051$

So, the relative lowering of vapour pressure is

$0.051$

Correct option: Option C.

If the calculated freezing point depression is $0.0197$ K, Van't Hoff factor (i) and degree of dissociation of acetic acid respectively are
questions.question_html: When $0.0106$ mole of acetic acid was dissolved in $1$ kg of water, the freezing point depression for this strength of acid was $0.0205$ K. If the calculated freezing point depression is $0.0197$ K, Van't Hoff factor (i) and degree of dissociation of acetic acid respectively are
questions.explanation_text: For solutions showing abnormal molar mass, Van’t Hoff factor is $i=\frac{\text{observed freezing point depression}}{\text{calculated freezing point depression}}$ Here, $\Delta T_{f}(\text{observed})=0.0205\text{K}$ and $\Delta T_{f}(\text{calculated})=0.0197\text{K}$ So, $i=\frac{0.0205}{0.0197}$ $i=1.041$ Acetic acid dissociates in water as $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_{3}\text{COO}^{-}+\text{H}^{+}$ One molecule gives $2$ particles on dissociation. For dissociation, $i=1+\alpha$ So, $\alpha=i-1$ $\alpha=1.041-1$ $\alpha=0.041$ Hence, the Van’t Hoff factor is $1.041$ and the degree of dissociation is $0.041$ . Correct option: D.
questions.explanation_html:
For solutions showing abnormal molar mass, Van’t Hoff factor is

$i=\frac{\text{observed freezing point depression}}{\text{calculated freezing point depression}}$

Here,

$\Delta T_{f}(\text{observed})=0.0205\text{K}$

and

$\Delta T_{f}(\text{calculated})=0.0197\text{K}$

So,

$i=\frac{0.0205}{0.0197}$

$i=1.041$

Acetic acid dissociates in water as

$\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_{3}\text{COO}^{-}+\text{H}^{+}$

One molecule gives $2$ particles on dissociation.

For dissociation,

$i=1+\alpha$

So,

$\alpha=i-1$

$\alpha=1.041-1$

$\alpha=0.041$

Hence, the Van’t Hoff factor is $1.041$ and the degree of dissociation is $0.041$ .

Correct option: D.

questions.explanation_text: Henry’s law states that the partial pressure of a gas in vapour phase is directly proportional to its mole fraction in the solution. So, $p=K_{H}\chi$ Hence, (a) Henry’s law matches with (ii). Raoult’s law states that the partial vapour pressure of a volatile component is equal to the product of its mole fraction and vapour pressure in pure state. So, $p_{1}=p_{1}^{0}x_{1}$ Hence, (b) Raoult’s law matches with (i). First law of thermodynamics is based on conservation of energy. It is written as $\Delta U=q+w$ Hence, (c) First law of thermodynamics matches with (iv). Kohlrausch’s law says that at infinite dilution, the molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of contributions of its ions. So, $\Lambda_{m}=v_{+}\lambda_{+}+v_{-}\lambda_{-}$ Hence, (d) Kohlrausch’s law matches with (iii). So the correct matching is: $a-ii,b-i,c-iv,d-iii$ Correct option: Option C.
questions.explanation_html:
Henry’s law states that the partial pressure of a gas in vapour phase is directly proportional to its mole fraction in the solution.

So,

$p=K_{H}\chi$

Hence,

(a) Henry’s law matches with (ii).

Raoult’s law states that the partial vapour pressure of a volatile component is equal to the product of its mole fraction and vapour pressure in pure state.

So,

$p_{1}=p_{1}^{0}x_{1}$

Hence,

(b) Raoult’s law matches with (i).

First law of thermodynamics is based on conservation of energy. It is written as

$\Delta U=q+w$

Hence,

(c) First law of thermodynamics matches with (iv).

Kohlrausch’s law says that at infinite dilution, the molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of contributions of its ions.

So,

$\Lambda_{m}=v_{+}\lambda_{+}+v_{-}\lambda_{-}$

Hence,

(d) Kohlrausch’s law matches with (iii).

So the correct matching is:

$a-ii,b-i,c-iv,d-iii$

Correct option: Option C.

questions.explanation_text: The correct option is Option D . For colligative properties, the number of solute particles is important. For osmotic pressure, $\pi=iCRT$ where $i$ is the van’t Hoff factor. NaCl dissociates in water: $\text{NaCl} \rightarrow \text{Na}^{+}+\text{Cl}^{-}$ So, for NaCl, $i \approx 2$ . Urea does not dissociate, so for urea, $i=1$ . Hence, for the same concentration, $\pi_{\text{NaCl}}>\pi_{\text{urea}}$ So Option A is incorrect. When salt is added to water, the vapour pressure of the solution decreases compared to pure water. So, $\text{Vapour pressure of salt water}<\text{Vapour pressure of pure water}$ Hence, Option D is correct .

questions.explanation_text: To determine which 0.1 m aqueous solution will have the lowest boiling point elevation, we need to consider the Van't Hoff factor ( $i$ ). This factor represents the number of particles the compound dissociates into in solution. The formula for boiling point elevation, $\Delta T_{b}∝i$ , indicates that a higher $i$ value leads to a greater elevation in boiling point. Here are the values of $i$ for each compound, assuming complete ionization: Aluminium chloride ( $AlCl_{3}$ ) : $i=4$ Aluminium sulfate ( $Al_{2}(SO_{4})_{3}$ ) : $i=5$ Potassium sulfate ( $K_{2}SO_{4}$ ) : $i=3$ Sodium chloride ( $NaCl$ ) : $i=2$ The solution with the lowest $i$ value will exhibit the smallest increase in boiling point. Therefore, sodium chloride, which has $i=2$ , will show the lowest boiling point elevation among the options.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question_text: 180 g of glucose, $C_{6}H_{12}O_{6}$ , is dissolved in 1 kg of water in a vessel. The temperature at which water boils at 1.013 bar is _________ (given, $K_{b}$ for water is $052Kkgmol^{-1}$ . Boiling point for pure water is 373.15 K )
questions.question_html: 180 g of glucose, $C_{6}H_{12}O_{6}$ , is dissolved in 1 kg of water in a vessel. The temperature at which water boils at 1.013 bar is _________ (given, $K_{b}$ for water is $052Kkgmol^{-1}$ . Boiling point for pure water is 373.15 K )
questions.explanation_text: To find the boiling point of the water solution, we need to calculate the boiling point elevation using the formula: $\Delta T_{b}=i \cdot K_{b} \cdot m$ where: $\Delta T_{b}$ is the boiling point elevation, $i$ is the van 't Hoff factor, which is 1 for glucose as it does not dissociate in solution, $K_{b}$ is the ebullioscopic constant for water, given as $0.52Kkgmol^{-1}$ , $m$ is the molality of the solution. To calculate the molality $m$ , use: $m=\frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{kilograms of solvent}}$ For glucose $(C_{6}H_{12}O_{6})$ , with a mass of 180 g: $\text{Moles of glucose}=\frac{180\text{g}}{180\text{g/mol}}=1\text{mol}$ The solvent (water) is 1 kg: $m=\frac{1\text{mol}}{1\text{kg}}=1\text{mol/kg}$ Substituting into the formula for $\Delta T_{b}$ : $\Delta T_{b}=1 \times 0.52 \times 1=0.52K$ The normal boiling point of pure water is 373.15 K. Therefore, the boiling point of the solution is: $T_{b}=373.15+0.52=373.67K$
questions.explanation_html:
To find the boiling point of the water solution, we need to calculate the boiling point elevation using the formula:

$\Delta T_{b}=i \cdot K_{b} \cdot m$

where:

$\Delta T_{b}$ is the boiling point elevation,

$i$ is the van 't Hoff factor, which is 1 for glucose as it does not dissociate in solution,

$K_{b}$ is the ebullioscopic constant for water, given as $0.52Kkgmol^{-1}$ ,

$m$ is the molality of the solution.

To calculate the molality $m$ , use:

$m=\frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{kilograms of solvent}}$

For glucose $(C_{6}H_{12}O_{6})$ , with a mass of 180 g:

$\text{Moles of glucose}=\frac{180\text{g}}{180\text{g/mol}}=1\text{mol}$

The solvent (water) is 1 kg:

$m=\frac{1\text{mol}}{1\text{kg}}=1\text{mol/kg}$

Substituting into the formula for $\Delta T_{b}$ :

$\Delta T_{b}=1 \times 0.52 \times 1=0.52K$

The normal boiling point of pure water is 373.15 K. Therefore, the boiling point of the solution is:

$T_{b}=373.15+0.52=373.67K$

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question_text: If $N_{2}$ gas is bubbled through water at 293 K , how many moles of $N_{2}$ gas would dissolve in 1 litre of water? Assume that $N_{2}$ exerts a partial pressure of 0.987 bar. [Given $K_{H}$ for $N_{2}$ at 293 K is 76.48 K bar ]
questions.question_html:
If $N_{2}$ gas is bubbled through water at 293 K , how many moles of $N_{2}$ gas would dissolve in 1 litre of water? Assume that $N_{2}$ exerts a partial pressure of 0.987 bar.

[Given $K_{H}$ for $N_{2}$ at 293 K is 76.48 K bar ]
questions.explanation_text: To determine the number of moles of $N_{2}$ gas that would dissolve in 1 liter of water at 293 K, when $N_{2}$ exerts a partial pressure of 0.987 bar, we can use Henry's Law. Given that the Henry's Law constant $(K_{H})$ for $N_{2}$ at 293 K is 76.48 K bar, we apply the following: Henry's Law $P=K_{H} \cdot X$ Where: $P$ is the partial pressure of the gas ( $0.987\text{bar}$ ), $K_{H}$ is Henry’s Law constant ( $76.48\text{K bar}$ ), $X$ is the mole fraction of the gas in the solvent. Calculating Mole Fraction of $N_{2}$ The mole fraction $X_{N_{2}}$ is given by: $X_{N_{2}}=\frac{P_{N_{2}}}{K_{H}}=\frac{0.987}{76.48 \times 10^{3}}=1.29 \times 10^{-5}$ Determining Moles of Water The number of moles of water ( $n_{H_{2}O}$ ) in 1 liter (1000 grams) is: $n_{H_{2}O}=\frac{1000}{18}=55.5$ Relating Mole Fraction and Moles of $N_{2}$ The mole fraction can also be expressed as: $X_{N_{2}}=\frac{n_{N_{2}}}{n_{N_{2}}+n_{H_{2}O}} \approx \frac{n_{N_{2}}}{55.5}$ Setting this equal to the previously calculated mole fraction: $1.29 \times 10^{-5}=\frac{n}{55.5}$ Solving for $n$ (the moles of $N_{2}$ ): $n_{N_{2}}=1.29 \times 10^{-5} \times 55.5=7.16 \times 10^{-4}$ Thus, the number of moles of $N_{2}$ gas dissolved in 1 liter of water is $7.16 \times 10^{-4}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
To determine the number of moles of $N_{2}$ gas that would dissolve in 1 liter of water at 293 K, when $N_{2}$ exerts a partial pressure of 0.987 bar, we can use Henry's Law. Given that the Henry's Law constant $(K_{H})$ for $N_{2}$ at 293 K is 76.48 K bar, we apply the following:

Henry's Law

$P=K_{H} \cdot X$

Where:

$P$ is the partial pressure of the gas ( $0.987\text{bar}$ ),

$K_{H}$ is Henry’s Law constant ( $76.48\text{K bar}$ ),

$X$ is the mole fraction of the gas in the solvent.

Calculating Mole Fraction of $N_{2}$

The mole fraction $X_{N_{2}}$ is given by:

$X_{N_{2}}=\frac{P_{N_{2}}}{K_{H}}=\frac{0.987}{76.48 \times 10^{3}}=1.29 \times 10^{-5}$

Determining Moles of Water

The number of moles of water ( $n_{H_{2}O}$ ) in 1 liter (1000 grams) is:

$n_{H_{2}O}=\frac{1000}{18}=55.5$

Relating Mole Fraction and Moles of $N_{2}$

The mole fraction can also be expressed as:

$X_{N_{2}}=\frac{n_{N_{2}}}{n_{N_{2}}+n_{H_{2}O}} \approx \frac{n_{N_{2}}}{55.5}$

Setting this equal to the previously calculated mole fraction:

$1.29 \times 10^{-5}=\frac{n}{55.5}$

Solving for $n$ (the moles of $N_{2}$ ):

$n_{N_{2}}=1.29 \times 10^{-5} \times 55.5=7.16 \times 10^{-4}$

Thus, the number of moles of $N_{2}$ gas dissolved in 1 liter of water is $7.16 \times 10^{-4}$ .

questions.explanation_text: Given, vapour pressure of pure liquid $A,p_{A}=450mm$ of $Hg$ vapour pressure of pure liquid $B$ , $p_{B}^{\circ}=700mm\text{of}Hg$ Total vapour pressure, $p_{\text{Total}}=600mm$ of $Hg$ From Raoult's law, $p_{\text{Total}}=p_{A}^{\circ}\chi_{A}+p_{B}\chi_{B}$ $\begin{aligned} & =p_{A}^{0}\chi_{A}+p_{B}^{0}(1-\chi_{A}) \\ \Rightarrow 600 & =450\chi_{A}=700(1-\chi_{A}) \\ & =450\chi_{A}+700-700\chi_{A} \\ & =700-250\chi_{A} \\ 250\chi_{A} & =700-600 \Rightarrow \chi_{A}=\frac{100}{250} \\ \chi_{A} & =0.4 \\ \therefore \chi_{B} & =1-0.4=0.6 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Henry's law constant for the solubility of $N_{2}$ gas in water at $298K$ is $1.0 \times 10^{5}atm$ . The mole fraction of $N_{2}$ in air is 0.8 . The number of moles of $N_{2}$ from air dissolved in 10 moles of water at $298K$ and $5atm$ pressure is
questions.question_html: Henry's law constant for the solubility of $N_{2}$ gas in water at $298K$ is $1.0 \times 10^{5}atm$ . The mole fraction of $N_{2}$ in air is 0.8 . The number of moles of $N_{2}$ from air dissolved in 10 moles of water at $298K$ and $5atm$ pressure is
questions.explanation_text: Given, Henry's law constant $(K_{H})$ for the solubility of $N_{2}$ gas in water at $298K=1 \times 10^{5}atm$ . Mole fraction of $N_{2}(\chi_{N_{2}})=0.8$ Hence, partial pressure of nitrogen, $\begin{aligned} p_{N_{2}} & =p_{\text{total}} \cdot \chi_{N_{2}} \\ & =0.8 \times 5atm \\ & =4atm \end{aligned}$ According to Henry's law, $\begin{aligned} p_{N_{2}} & =K_{H}\chi_{N_{2}} \\ 4 & =10^{5} \cdot \chi_{N_{2}} \\ \chi_{N_{2}} & =4 \times 10^{-5} \end{aligned}$ We know that, $\begin{aligned} \chi_{N_{2}} & =\frac{n_{N_{2}}}{n_{N_{2}}+n_{H_{2}O}} \\ 4 \times 10^{-5} & =\frac{n_{N_{2}}}{10}( \because n_{N_{2}}<<n_{H_{2}O}) \\ \Rightarrow n_{N_{2}} & =4 \times 10^{-4}\text{moles} \end{aligned}$ Thus, the number of moles of $N_{2}$ from air dissolved in 10 moles of water at $295K$ and $5atm$ pressure is $4 \times 10^{-4}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Given, Henry's law constant $(K_{H})$ for the solubility of $N_{2}$ gas in water at $298K=1 \times 10^{5}atm$ .

Mole fraction of $N_{2}(\chi_{N_{2}})=0.8$

Hence, partial pressure of nitrogen,

$\begin{aligned} p_{N_{2}} & =p_{\text{total}} \cdot \chi_{N_{2}} \\ & =0.8 \times 5atm \\ & =4atm \end{aligned}$

According to Henry's law,

$\begin{aligned} p_{N_{2}} & =K_{H}\chi_{N_{2}} \\ 4 & =10^{5} \cdot \chi_{N_{2}} \\ \chi_{N_{2}} & =4 \times 10^{-5} \end{aligned}$

We know that,

$\begin{aligned} \chi_{N_{2}} & =\frac{n_{N_{2}}}{n_{N_{2}}+n_{H_{2}O}} \\ 4 \times 10^{-5} & =\frac{n_{N_{2}}}{10}( \because n_{N_{2}}<<n_{H_{2}O}) \\ \Rightarrow n_{N_{2}} & =4 \times 10^{-4}\text{moles} \end{aligned}$

Thus, the number of moles of $N_{2}$ from air dissolved in 10 moles of water at $295K$ and $5atm$ pressure is $4 \times 10^{-4}$ .

questions.explanation_text: Relative lowering of vapor pressure is defined as: $\frac{p^{0}-p}{p^{0}}$ For dilute solutions, this can be approximated by Raoult's law: $\frac{p^{0}-p}{p^{0}}=\frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{n_{\text{solvent}}}$ Given that the relative lowering of vapor pressure is 0.002: $0.002=\frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{n_{\text{solvent}}}$ Since the solvent is water, with $1kg$ of water: $n_{\text{solvent}}=\frac{1000}{18} \approx 55.56\text{mol}$ Let $n_{\text{solute}}$ be the moles of glucose. Then: $0.002=\frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{55.56}$ Solving for $n_{\text{solute}}$ : $n_{\text{solute}}=0.002 \times 55.56 \approx 0.111\text{mol}$ The molality (m) is defined as moles of solute per kilogram of solvent: $\text{Molality}=\frac{0.111\text{mol}}{1\text{kg}}=0.111\text{m}$ Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C: 0.111
questions.explanation_html:
Relative lowering of vapor pressure is defined as:

$\frac{p^{0}-p}{p^{0}}$

For dilute solutions, this can be approximated by Raoult's law:

$\frac{p^{0}-p}{p^{0}}=\frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{n_{\text{solvent}}}$

Given that the relative lowering of vapor pressure is 0.002:

$0.002=\frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{n_{\text{solvent}}}$

Since the solvent is water, with $1kg$ of water:

$n_{\text{solvent}}=\frac{1000}{18} \approx 55.56\text{mol}$

Let $n_{\text{solute}}$ be the moles of glucose. Then:

$0.002=\frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{55.56}$

Solving for $n_{\text{solute}}$ :

$n_{\text{solute}}=0.002 \times 55.56 \approx 0.111\text{mol}$

The molality (m) is defined as moles of solute per kilogram of solvent:

$\text{Molality}=\frac{0.111\text{mol}}{1\text{kg}}=0.111\text{m}$

Therefore, the correct answer is:

Option C: 0.111
